title: Irregular verbs; lie and lay, sit and set, rise and raise
blurb: Use the right past and past participle of common irregular verbs, and never mix up lie and lay, sit and set, or rise and raise.
question: A shift note reads, “Mr. Diaz laid in bed all morning, so the aide sat his lunch tray beside him and rose the head of the bed. He had ate only half by noon.” Which verbs are wrong, and what should they be?

teach.h: Three forms to know for every verb
teach.body: Formally, every verb has principal parts: the base (go), the simple past (went) and the past participle (gone), which follows has, have or had. Regular verbs add -ed for both past forms (walk, walked, walked); irregular verbs change in their own ways and must be memorized. Plain English: the past form stands alone (“She went”); the participle needs a helper (“She has gone”). The HESI A2 tests the pairs people swap.

teach.caption: Same three forms on a test: “I saw” (past, alone) but “I have seen” (participle, with a helper). Never “I seen” or “I have saw.”

teach.h: Past alone, participle with a helper
teach.note: Nonstandard forms to reject on sight: brung, throwed, drug (for dragged), had went, has came, had ate, has wrote.

teach.caption: The “a” verbs (lay, set, raise) act on an object: lay the chart, set the tray, raise the bed. Lie, sit and rise take no object.

teach.h: Rise vs raise, sit vs set

teach.h: Scenario: Priya corrects a shift note
teach.body: CNA and nursing applicant Priya Shah reviews: “Mr. Diaz laid in bed all morning, so the aide sat his lunch tray beside him and rose the head of the bed. He had ate only half by noon.” Reclining takes no object, so “lay in bed.” A tray is placed, so “set his lunch tray.” The bed is lifted, so “raised the head of the bed.” After “had,” use the participle: “had eaten.” Four verbs, four fixes.

teach.text: “Lay” is BOTH the present of lay and the past of lie, which is why it is the most tested verb on the HESI A2. “Yesterday I lay down” is correct; “Yesterday I laid down” is wrong because nothing was put down. “The chart has laid there all day” is wrong too: the chart is resting, so “has lain.”

items: Past forms stand alone (saw, went, took); past participles follow has, have or had (seen, gone, taken).
Learn irregular verbs in sets of three: begin, began, begun; freeze, froze, frozen.
Lie (recline): lie, lay, lain. Lay (put): lay, laid, laid.
Sit and rise take no object; set and raise act on something.
Reject nonstandard forms: brung, throwed, had went, I seen, could of.

summary: You can now give the past and past participle of the irregular verbs the HESI A2 uses most and match each to the right helper. You can also choose lie or lay, sit or set, and rise or raise by asking whether the verb acts on an object.

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “By the time the doctor arrived, the patient had ___ his whole breakfast.”
A.why: After “had,” use the past participle. The forms are eat, ate, eaten, so “had eaten.”

whyNot.0: “Ate” is the simple past and cannot follow “had.”
whyNot.2: “Eat” is irregular; “eated” is not a standard form.
whyNot.3: “Eat” is the base form and cannot follow “had.”

A.q: Which sentence uses the verb form correctly?
options: I seen the updated policy on the staff board.
She has went to the pharmacy for the refill.
The bell had rang before the exam started.
They have written their essays for the program.
A.why: “Have” needs the past participle, and “written” is the past participle of “write.”

whyNot.0: “Seen” is a past participle and needs a helper: “I saw” or “I have seen.”
whyNot.1: After “has,” the participle “gone” is needed: “she has gone.”
whyNot.2: After “had,” the participle “rung” is needed: “had rung.”

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “After the long shift, Jamal ___ down on the couch and slept for an hour.”
A.why: Jamal reclined (no object), so the verb is “lie.” Its past tense is “lay,” matching the past “slept.”

whyNot.1: “Laid” is the past of “lay” (to put something down) and needs an object.
whyNot.2: “Lied” is the past of “lie” meaning to tell an untruth.
whyNot.3: “Layed” is not a standard form; the past of “lay” is “laid.”

B.q: Which sentence about the patient's chart is correct?
options: She lay the chart on the counter before rounds.
She laid down for a nap before her night shift.
She has lain the chart on the counter already.
She laid the chart on the counter before rounds.
B.why: Putting the chart down takes an object, so the verb is “lay”; its past is “laid.”

whyNot.0: “Lay” here would be the past of “lie,” which takes no object; the past of “lay” is “laid.”
whyNot.1: Napping takes no object, so the past of “lie” is needed: “she lay down.”
whyNot.2: “Lain” is the participle of “lie” (recline); with an object, use “has laid.”

B.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The committee has ___ six applicants for interviews next week.”
B.why: After “has,” use the past participle. Choose, chose, chosen: “has chosen.”

whyNot.0: “Chose” is the simple past and cannot follow “has.”
whyNot.1: “Choose” is irregular; “choosed” is not a standard form.
whyNot.2: “Choose” is the base form and cannot follow “has.”

options: Please set down in the waiting room until called.
The patient has set by the window all afternoon.
The aide sat the water pitcher on the bedside table.
The aide set the water pitcher on the bedside table.
B.why: “Set” means to place something and takes an object (the water pitcher); its past is also “set.”

whyNot.0: Taking a seat has no object, so the verb is “sit”: “please sit down.”
whyNot.1: Being seated has no object, so the participle of “sit” is needed: “has sat.”
whyNot.2: Placing a pitcher takes an object, so the verb is “set,” not “sat.”

C.q: Which sentence uses the correct past participle?
options: The pipes had froze overnight, so the clinic opened late.
The lab tech has broken two slides since Monday morning.
The toddler had tore the paper gown before the exam.
The students had swam laps before their morning class.
C.why: Break, broke, broken: “has” needs the past participle “broken.”

C.q: Which sentence uses the verb correctly?
options: Please raise the head of the bed before meals.
The patient tried to raise from the chair slowly.
Her blood pressure raised sharply after the news.
Clinic fees have raised every year since 2020.
C.why: “Raise” takes an object (the head of the bed), so “raise” is correct.

whyNot.1: Getting up takes no object, so the verb is “rise”: “tried to rise.”
whyNot.2: Blood pressure goes up by itself (no object), so the verb is “rose.”
whyNot.3: Fees going up takes no object, so the verb is “rise”: “have risen.”

C.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? “After she had laid on the couch for an hour, Rina rose and set her mug in the sink.”
C.why: Rina was resting (no object), so the verb is “lie,” and after “had” its participle is “lain”: “had lain on the couch.”

whyNot.0: “Had” is the correct helper for the earlier of two past actions.
whyNot.2: “Rose” is the correct past of “rise”: she got up, with no object.
whyNot.3: “Set” is correct: she placed something (her mug).

reteach.title: Two families at the bedside
reteach.question: Imagine two families of verbs at a patient's bedside: one family rests, the other family handles things. How do you tell which family a sentence needs?

blocks.body: The resting family (lie, sit, rise) only does things to itself: the patient lies down, sits up, rises from the chair. The handling family (lay, set, raise) always handles something: the aide lays the gown out, sets the tray down, raises the bed. Before you choose, look for the thing being handled. If there is one, call the handler; if not, call the rester. Then pick the right time form.

blocks.text: The resting verb “lie” borrows the handler's word “lay” for its past tense. When you see “lay,” check the time: if it is yesterday and nothing is being placed, “lay” is correct.

explain.body: The simple past stands alone (She took the course). The past participle follows has, have or had (She has taken the course). Irregular verbs often use a different word for each.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The new aide has already ___ the infection-control course.”
test.why: After “has,” use the past participle. Take, took, taken: “has taken.”

whyNot.0: “Took” is the simple past and cannot follow “has.”
whyNot.2: “Take” is irregular; “taked” is not a standard form.
whyNot.3: “Take” is the base form and cannot follow “has.”

explain.body: Lie means to recline and takes no object: lie, lay, lain, lying. Lay means to put something down and takes an object: lay, laid, laid, laying.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The dog has ___ by the front door since the visitors left.”
test.why: The dog is resting (no object), so the verb is “lie.” After “has,” use its participle “lain.”

whyNot.0: “Laid” belongs to “lay” (put something) and needs an object.
whyNot.1: “Lay” is the simple past of “lie” and cannot follow “has.”

explain.body: Sit means to be seated (no object): sit, sat, sat. Set means to place something (object): set, set, set.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The patient ___ in the recliner for an hour after her treatment yesterday.”
test.why: Being seated takes no object, and “yesterday” calls for the past: “sat.”

whyNot.0: “Set” means to place something and needs an object.
whyNot.2: “Sit” is present tense, but the sentence is about yesterday.
whyNot.3: “Seated” needs a helper or an object (“was seated,” “seated herself”).

explain.body: Rise means to go up by itself (no object): rise, rose, risen. Raise means to lift something (object): raise, raised, raised.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The patient's temperature has ___ two degrees since this morning.”
test.why: A temperature goes up by itself (no object), so the verb is “rise.” After “has,” use “risen.”

whyNot.0: “Raised” belongs to “raise,” which needs an object.
whyNot.1: “Rose” is the simple past and cannot follow “has.”
whyNot.2: “Rise” is irregular; “rised” is not a standard form.
